newsitem.title: JAPAN: Nintendo interim profits seen taking steep dive.
newsitem.headline: Nintendo interim profits seen taking steep dive.

text.p: A shift to new-generation game players is likely to slash Nintendo Co Ltd's profits in half when the videogame giant announces its half-year results early next month, analysts say.

But the launch back in June of the smarter and faster 64-bit game machine, the N64, will likely boost the company's Christmas season sales, they said, although it came too late to stop a slip in parent profits in the April-September period.
"It's just in an off-crop season," said Takanobu Murakami, an analyst at Yamaichi Research Institute of Securities and Economics.

Nintendo's N64 players are likely to battle head-to-head with Sony Corp's PlayStation in the Christmas season, outperforming Sega Enterprise Ltd's Saturn player, said SBC Warburg Securities Japan analyst Reinier Dobbelmann.
Nintendo will announce its parent-only results for the six months to September, the first half of the business year ending next March 31, on November 6.

Nintendo's president, Hiroshi Yamauchi, recently told reporters its parent current profit will likely be 30 billion yen ($267 million) in the first half, against 63.87 billion yen ($570 million) in the same period a year ago.
Current profit is pretax and includes gains or losses on non-operating activities such as investment in stocks.

Nintendo's profits are being hurt in the short-term because the launch of the new, higher-performance player has resulted in falling prices for software for Nintendo's old SuperFamicon player, which is still the company's mainstay product.

Rival game maker Sony will announce its results on November 7. Analysts say its group-based profits for the half-year period will show a jump to 41 billion yen ($369 million) from 16.09 billion yen ($144 million) in the same period last year.
Analysts are closely watching Nintendo's second-half performance as the year-end gift-giving season typically accounts for 60 percent of videogame makers' sales.
"Sony is doing much better than I forecast. This may be the peak year for PlayStation sales," Dobbelmann said.
Dobbelmann said he expects 2.7 million N64s to be sold in Japan by March 1997, although the figure could change slightly depending on the balance of Japanese and U.S. market sales.
Another Yamaichi Research analyst, Akira Namikawa, expects Sony to to sell more than three million PlayStations by the end of next March.
Sega's Saturn will have sales at home of only about 1.2 million units by the end of March, or only half the company's target, Dobbelmann predicted.
But despite the slower-than-expected sales in Saturn hardware, Sega will manage to maintain its year-ago profit levels, analysts said.
"Profits from videogame arcades and from sales of machines to those arcades are increasing," said Namikawa.
He estimates videogame arcades operated by Sega will show a sales rise of 15 percent to 16 percent for the April-September period compared with the same period a a year ago.
Namikawa expects Sega to report 12 billion yen ($107 million) in parent current profit in the first half, compared to 11.04 billion yen ($98.5 million) a year ago.
Sega will announce parent-only results for the first half-year period in late November. ($1=112 yen)
